questions.q: What is the purpose of a collection bucket in the GTD system?
a: To capture interruptions and tasks so your mind can stay focused
To rank your tasks by how urgent they are
To store finished projects for later review
To schedule every task into a calendar slot
questions.why: Lesson 1 says the bucket holds whatever lands in your brain or lap while you work.

questions.q: What belongs on a next actions list, according to Allen?
a: Specific tasks that take less than 30 minutes
Every task you hope to finish this year
Only tasks that need another person's input
Long projects broken into monthly milestones
questions.why: Lesson 2 defines next actions as the specific tasks of current projects, each under 30 minutes.

questions.q: Why does Allen suggest sorting next action lists by place, like laptop or phone?
a: So you can pick a task that fits wherever you are
So you can measure how long each task takes
So you can delegate tasks more easily to others
So you never repeat the same task twice
questions.why: Lesson 2 gives the airport example: a notebook list still works when wifi and battery are gone.

questions.q: How often does Allen say you should empty your collection buckets?
a: About once a week
At the end of every day
Only when they are completely full
Once at the start of each month
questions.why: Lesson 1 says the system only works if the bucket is emptied regularly, ideally weekly.

questions.q: Why is the weekly review essential to the GTD system?
a: Lists only help if they are kept up to date
It is the only time you may add new tasks
It replaces the need for a collection bucket
It shows which tasks you should drop entirely
questions.why: Lesson 3 says lists are only as good as they are current, so the review keeps everything complete.
